summary.text: An estuary is a partly enclosed coastal body of brackish water where fresh water from rivers or streams mixes with salt water from the open sea.
That mixing brings high levels of nutrients, making estuaries among the most productive natural habitats in the world and nurseries for many young fish and shellfish.
Most of today's estuaries formed when the sea began rising about 10,000 to 12,000 years ago and flooded valleys carved by rivers or glaciers.

facts.label: Name origin
facts.value: Latin aestuarium, tidal inlet, from aestus, tide

facts.label: Commonest temperate type
facts.value: Drowned river valley, or coastal plain estuary

facts.label: US examples
facts.value: Hudson River, Chesapeake Bay, Delaware Bay, Tampa Bay

facts.label: Glacial type
facts.value: Fjords: U-shaped valleys deepened by glaciers

items.prompt: You scoop a cup of water where a river widens and meets the tide. What would you expect it to taste like?

options.label: Mildly salty, a blend of fresh and sea
Completely fresh, like the upstream river
Salty only on stormy days, fresh otherwise
Just like open ocean water, unchanged

items.explain: An estuary holds brackish water: seawater coming in is diluted by fresh water from rivers and streams.

items.prompt: Estuaries rank among the most productive natural habitats on Earth. What mainly drives all that life?

options.label: Warm currents rising from the deep ocean
Fresh and sea water mixing, rich in nutrients
A total lack of predators in brackish water
Constant sunlight that never reaches the seabed

items.explain: Mixing seawater and freshwater supplies high levels of nutrients in the water and sediment.

items.prompt: Roughly when did most of the world's existing estuaries come into being?

options.label: About 100 million years ago
About 2 million years ago
About 10,000 to 12,000 years ago
About 500 years ago

items.explain: Most formed in the Holocene, when rising seas flooded river-eroded or glacier-scoured valleys about 10,000 to 12,000 years ago.

items.prompt: In a temperate lowland, the sea slowly creeps inland up the old course of a stream, and the flooded inlet keeps the stream's shape. What type of estuary is this?

options.label: A fjord
A bar-built estuary
A river delta
A coastal plain estuary

items.explain: Drowned river valleys, also called coastal plain estuaries, form as rising sea water penetrates a valley; they are the commonest type in temperate climates.

items.prompt: A shallow subtropical estuary sits cut off from the ocean behind a chain of barrier islands. How did it most likely form?

options.label: Sediment piled up as fast as the sea rose
A glacier gouged out a deep, steep trough
A volcanic crater filled with seawater
The river dried up and the sea moved in

items.explain: Bar-built estuaries form where sediment deposition keeps pace with rising seas, leaving them shallow behind spits or barrier islands.

items.prompt: A coastal town asks whether the salt marsh grass fringing its estuary is worth protecting. What does that grass do for the town?

options.label: Raises salt levels so fishing improves
Holds the shore and softens storm impacts
Speeds erosion by trapping waves
Blocks tides from entering the estuary

items.explain: Salt marsh grasses stabilize shorelines and reduce erosion, buffering storms and sea-level rise and protecting infrastructure.

paragraphs.heading: Where river meets sea
paragraphs.text: An estuary is a partly enclosed body of brackish water on the coast, where fresh water from rivers or streams mixes with salt water from the sea. It is a transition zone between river and ocean, and so counts as an ecotone, a place where different ecosystems overlap. Both sides shape it: the sea through tides, waves and salty water pushing inland, and the river through its flow of fresh water and the sediment it brings.

paragraphs.heading: Pinning down a definition
paragraphs.text: The word comes from the Latin aestuarium, a tidal inlet of the sea, itself from aestus, meaning tide. The most widely accepted definition describes a semi-enclosed coastal water body with a free link to the open sea, where sea water is measurably diluted by fresh water draining off the land. That leaves out coastal lagoons and brackish seas, so a broader definition lets the fresh water inflow stop at times, the sea link close for part of the year, and the tides have little effect. Under the broader version, fjords, lagoons, river mouths and tidal creeks all count.

paragraphs.heading: Tides, mixing and nutrients
paragraphs.text: Sea water enters an estuary with the rhythm of the tides and is diluted by water from rivers and streams. How that dilution plays out differs from one estuary to the next, depending on how much fresh water arrives, the tidal range, and how much water evaporates. The mixing also delivers plenty of nutrients, in the water and in the sediment, which makes estuaries some of the most productive natural habitats in the world.

paragraphs.heading: Nurseries and natural filters
paragraphs.text: Freshwater, marine and land species live side by side in estuaries and build complex food webs. Many marine fish and shellfish spend their early lives there, and estuaries also support mangroves, seagrasses, salt marshes and seaweeds. Migratory birds and endangered species find habitat there too. Wetlands such as swamps and salt marshes filter the sediment, nutrients and pollutants washed down from upland areas, and marsh grasses hold shorelines in place, cushioning storms and sea-level rise.

paragraphs.heading: How estuaries formed
paragraphs.text: Most estuaries today date from the Holocene, when the sea began to rise about 10,000 to 12,000 years ago and flooded valleys cut by rivers or scoured by glaciers. The commonest type in temperate climates is the drowned river valley, also called a coastal plain estuary, where rising sea water creeps up a river valley and the estuary keeps the valley's shape; Chesapeake Bay is one. Bar-built estuaries form where sediment has piled up as fast as the sea rose, leaving shallow water cut off from the ocean by sand spits or barrier islands. Fjords formed where Pleistocene glaciers deepened and widened river valleys into a U shape.

paragraphs.heading: Under pressure
paragraphs.text: Many estuaries are in decline. Causes include soil erosion, deforestation, overgrazing, overfishing and the filling-in of wetlands. Other pressures are eutrophication linked to excess nutrients from nitrogen runoff, sewage and animal waste; pollutants such as heavy metals, polychlorinated biphenyls, radionuclides and hydrocarbons from sewage; and dikes or dams built for flood control or water diversion.
